utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, it wasn't your job to take these persons' statements, but to interview them and make a note. Now, you didn't ask those persons to sign it; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Where I was, we only worked with Official Notes, and that's where our contact with those written materials ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That means that the persons who came to you didn't sign statements but you only made an Official Note of the interview?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it was only transmitted in this form, the form of an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the last page of this document, which is page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the last paragraph, where we see that Official Notes were made. Just as you said. So statements weren't taken from these persons, but, rather, Official Notes were attached.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: That is possible. I haven't seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 3 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the paragraph. Above "the reasoning," it says that: On 24 May 1992, around 1430 at Jakupovici, on the main road Banja Luka-Prijedor, these persons carried out an armed attack on a military column when Jova Zgonjanin, a soldier, was killed. Do you remember that this was a matter of interest to you to see who took part in that attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this column was also discussed, that some of the detainees were interviewed about that. But I cannot say with certainty what person this was about. But, certainly, this incident was also of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that while taking the statements you also received information about armed units and their activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did get such information about units and possibly some activities of theirs and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you certainly put that down in your Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Information about persons, their weapons, their organisation, and anything that related to that unconstitutional or illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you take a look at page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Down by the bottom of the page. The members of public security were offered to sign a declaration of loyalty to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we then please see page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm reading: "Staff of Muslim ethnicity from the police department of Kozarac was subject to pressure -- or, rather, pressurised not to sign the loyalty declaration." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I don't remember this specific instance, but we focussed on -- our -- we focussed our attention on any person of Serb or Muslim ethnicity who seemed to exert negative influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This incident which happened on 25 April was a prelude to the events in the Prijedor municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I think that was one of the events that triggered some those activities. There were more, but this would have been the culmination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence. Given my line of questioning, I will tender only one criminal report as an example. I will not tender all others. It will serve as an example of the way they worked at the time and the Official Notes which are included in this criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours there seems to be a lack of foundation here. There's no evidence here that these persons listed in this criminal report were detained at Keraterm, whether they were interviewed by this witness or one of the teams at Keraterm. And we have to recall that the issue that I believe was at the start of Mr. Krgovic's questions was whether the information they were obtaining at Keraterm somehow made it into or resulted into a criminal report, and that has -- that link hasn't been established in this document. The Prosecution is not contending that -- that non-Serbs were arrested and criminal reports were filed against them in 1992, and that's really all this shows. And with regard to the last line of questions, this witness has said that doesn't require the incident -- he doesn't recall the incident that Mr. Krgovic is referring him to. So I don't think the foundation is established for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to go into details now. I can show this document to the witness again and ask him, Do you remember this person, or that person, but that would be a waste of time. My line of questioning was why the witness took part in these activity, what the purpose was, and what happened to these Official Notes. And now we see that the Official Notes are included in this part. That's in line with what the witness said, that they didn't take statement, only made notes. At least his part of the team. And he remembers the events and the testimonies of the people who participated in these events. Maybe not specifically, but he remembers on a -- at a general level. So I believe that there is a -- a link.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But. Your Honours, he hasn't shown one part of this document that mentions Keraterm or that any persons in here was detained at Keraterm. So -- and this witness had very little additional information to add with regard to this document other than maybe he recalls a few of the events that it reports on. And those events I believe are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, doesn't it appear that this document is, as it were, just there, in relation to this witness's testimony? There's no nexus, is there, apart from his general awareness of the events to which it speaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence submits that the purpose of these Official Notes and the events that the witness remembers were used to produce these -- this criminal report, and that was the -- the work of the state security and the public security. The people who were brought in for investigation were brought in for a reason, namely, participation in armed rebellion. And that's what I want to prove through this document. I can go through this document and show the witness some names to hear whether he remembers the people or the events, but I was trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is precisely it because this witness has given evidence that he doesn't have any recollection of any of his -- any of the information contained in his Official Notes making it into a criminal report or resulting in a criminal report filed against any of the detainees. He said that heard that down the road maybe there was some, but that's all he knew. This document doesn't get us any further to where the Defence wants to go because there's nothing in here that mentions that these persons were detained at Keraterm or that this witness was the one who interviewed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you may succeed in persuading us that this document should be admitted, but the link is not yet established, not through this witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, let me just ask you the following: The purpose of your stay in Prijedor was -- sorry, at Keraterm, was that you, as a part of a team, collect information about armed rebellion and the organisation and structure of what was then called paramilitary units of the Muslim and Croat side?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, as part of your work, you made Official Notes, precisely about those circumstances, arming and some incidents involving fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, arming, procurements, and armed incidents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witnesses is kindly asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, again, the interpreters need you to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you took statements about the military organisation in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Kozarac, among other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in this context, you also investigated the activities of Sead Cirkin from Kozarusa and the group that was organised in Kozarusa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I remember Cirkin from this list because he was a leader of this whole effort and the master mind. I remember him. I don't remember the others. And I remember that even Bosniaks said that this was a person with a murky past who threatened them too. So this is all I remember. If, perhaps -- no, I'm sorry, I think that Cirkin was, in fact, a serviceman in the army, and the other one was Kusuran.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 1 of this document. I think we are talking about the person listed under number 2 here. Suljo Kusuran.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he had this murky past, and he acted in a brazen manner. And I think that Cirkin was, in fact, a military serviceman and that he dealt with the military organisation. I don't remember any of the others, given that a long time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in the notes that you took, those two persons were identified as the master minds of this group?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Bosniaks, mostly Bosniaks, spoke of them in those terms, saying that they took part in the logistical effort and the other one perhaps in the military part. Perhaps I don't recall exactly, but it was mostly in that sense; that's how they were characterised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this information, you wrote them down in your notes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, if we obtained this information, we recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that we have established a basis for the tendering of this document because the -- the witness spoke about the investigation carried out regarding these two persons who are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're no closer to the link that needs to be established here. We seem to be going in circles, in fact. If the Defence is interested in what happened in Kozarac in 1992, he certainly can ask the witness what happened and what information he obtained from detainees at Keraterm. That's completely fair questioning. But here is a document, again, a criminal report, that should show no connection between the work that this witness did and the result of this report because there's no link that says that this report was filed based upon interviews conducted at Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, it's time for the break. We would rule on the application to admit it when we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I should preface the promised ruling by saying that, reluctantly, we are persuaded, Mr. Krgovic, that the document may be admitted and marked at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, I have some computer problems here, so I don't have LiveNote on my screen, but we'll be using the main screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, the Prosecutor asked you about the number of statements taken -- or, rather, I apologise, the number of persons that you interviewed over a certain period of time. And now I will show you this document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P657. I need page 8 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here, it is stated that over 200 -- or, rather, 900 persons were processed, operatively, and I think that based on your testimony that's what you said, that this is the number of persons -- the approximate number of persons that were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant exclusively the Keraterm area. So if this document was dated sometime in the middle of that period the -- the total figure was a bit higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could you give us an estimate for the overall period?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you that I couldn't give you the exact number. We didn't have any statistics. But the number was about 20 to 25 interviews a day, three teams, over a period of maybe 65 days or so. So this was the methodology that I used, pure mathematics. But I can't give you the exact figure because we didn't keep accurate records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, the Prosecutor asked you about the situation in Prijedor on the eve of the war and all the other activities there. My question is: From the 13th [as interpreted] of April when Prijedor was declared a Serb municipality, when the military and other forces took over some of the positions there, until the incidents in Hambarine and Kozarac and the attack on Prijedor, there were no clashes, no conflicts in the area of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall any significant clashes. There may have been some incidents but no conflicts, no clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just note for the record that it says the takeover was on the "13th of April." I think he meant to say the "30th of April."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have LiveNote, so I cannot follow the transcript. But, yes, the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when these people were brought in for questioning in the reception centres, this was the result of the combat operations in those areas from which those people were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, some of the activities pertaining to the bringing of these people into custody started after those events and with those events. But the establishment of the centres, well, this tells you everything you need to know. They were established on the 25th of May, if I got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And before that date, there was no fighting. So before those attacks in Hambarine and Kozarac and the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, there were no clashes between the Serb army and the military in the area where there were Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there were any such activities in that period, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you do know that sometime in late May there was an attack on Prijedor by a Muslim unit commanded by Slavko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall the date, but I do know that in that period the reception centres, the camps, were already in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that there were some initial successes in this attack and that the Muslim-Croat units reached the town centre close to the police station and the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I know that because that morning we were unable to go to our job as usual because there were some -- there was some fighting and it was dangerous to move for individuals or small groups because there was some shooting around the SUP building. That was the reason why I was unable to go to work on the day, and none of my colleagues was able to get to work. I spent that day at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, now I will show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 2D03-1189.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That speaks about the event, the attack on Prijedor, to see whether you know anything about the persons and events described therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D03-1189. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that military security was involved in taking those statements.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a representative, a member, there. Now, I don't know whether you can characterise what he did as working on it. He was present there. That much I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you made those Official Notes, later on, after the attack on Prijedor, one of the topics that you discussed with these people was the attack and the formations that took part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, similar to the initial part. We tried to talk to the people about this, and they told us what they knew about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at this criminal report, page 1. It's a criminal report against Asim Muhic, Kemal Alagic, and two other people who are on this list.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Suad Karagic, a man named as Big Ed, and then another man nicknamed Politicki.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recall making Official Notes with any of these people?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I can't recall anything about the persons listed under number 3, but I do know that it happened with persons listed under 1 and 3 -- 1 and 2 because they were leaders, in a way. In the first case, the situation was somewhat similar. I think that Asim Muhic was an active -- a military person, but then he left the army. And Kemal Alagic was a criminal. He had a criminal record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do we have the English version of what you're discussing with the witness in front of us? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now we have. Perhaps. The first page I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to page 1. I'm sorry, I don't have the e-court and I don't have LiveNote on my screen, so I'm unable to follow what's going on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be, once again, asked to make a short pause before answering each of Mr. Krgovic's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, this describes in detail the attack, how the attack proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 2 of this document, so how the attack progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here it says that this person, Asim Muhic, and Kemal Alagic, together with Slavko Ecimovic ... That's the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As the platoon commander and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters are asking to you slow down when reading. And, Mr. Rodic, the interpreters remind you to allow a pause between the question and your attempt to answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Rodic. Now take a look at the second paragraph, which reads: In the attack on Prijedor, there was this first platoon led by Kemal Alagic had a difficult task, the attack on the -- on the municipality and the police, and then the members of the groups are listed and their weapons. And then there is Slavko Ecimovic's group, whose task was to take the reserve officers' hall, the Prijedor hotel, the bridge over the Sana, and the radio station. The second group was supposed to reach the management buildings of the Ljubija mines. And the third group was supposed to cut the road leading to the barracks where the army was. There was also a fourth group that was supposed to secure the buildings taken, that is, the Sana bridge and the Prijedor hotel. Do you remember that this hotel was burnt during one of those attacks?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I did not pass by the hotel at that time. But later, I saw that it was burning, and I heard that it happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the attack had come from, geographically speaking, from which direction the Muslim forces had come?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, they had crossed the Sana, which means that they had come from the villages of Hambarine, Biscani. I don't remember exactly. Anyway, they crossed the Sana, and that's how they reached these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your indulgence, I will try to log on LiveNote because I cannot follow the transcript or the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have done part of the job, but it still isn't functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 65 ter 3111. It's a map which is, at the same time, Exhibit P1216.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a map of Prijedor. We have seen the locations. Can you tell us or mark on the map from which direction they crossed the Sana and reached the centre of Prijedor? If you can. Or, actually, I'm afraid that this is the wrong map. Is this map sufficient for you to indicate from which direction they came?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, we got some information through the interviews, and some information from the -- from those involved. So I cannot be precise as to what I heard from who. But, if I may, I'll mark this village here, Rizvanovici. From this direction, they may have crossed the Sana at one place. And then they deployed to toward the hotel here. And then in this direction. I don't know how clear this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the third group which was mentioned and advanced along the banks?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't quite remember. But I think they crossed the Sana, and they came here, and then they went upstream toward the hotel. The other went to the officers' hall. And the third one took a roundabout way and went to the Puharska neighbourhood, and they tried to cut the road between the Urija neighbourhood and the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark these groups, one, two, and three?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which was which. One was here. Another was here. And up there, there was a third.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any casualties on the Serb side then?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I know that there were casualties. Conditionally speaking, there were colleagues from the MUP, outside the MUP building. There were was acquaintances of mine from my school days, at secondary school. I think I knew somebody who got killed in front of the hotel, but I couldn't say how many people exactly got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the rest of the group? Once the attack ended, where did that group return to? Was there street fighting on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: What I'm about to say originates from some interviews and some information I observed personally, and probably heard the stories of some people who were on the other side. Namely, that these locations were taken until the army arrived - or the police; don't take my word for it - from the direction of Urija. That's when the combat began. And then they started to retreat to their initial positions; that is, they went through the Stari Grad neighbourhood. There they offered some resistance, but they were pushed back over the Sana again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate where -- the whereabouts of Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: It would be roughly where the crossing over the Sana is. I will mark it more boldly. This is where the Sana is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicated it with a number 4.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, here you here. I'm afraid it isn't all too clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that day when this fighting took place there was also fighting inside Stari Grad itself and that a large number of houses was damaged during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that from direct experience because I live very nearby. I couldn't see the fighting itself, but I heard it because it's only some 700 or 800 metres away from where I live, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Some of these people who pulled out crossed the Sana, went to the surrounding villages, and mingled with the local population; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: We got some of the that information from the people we interviewed, that they had crossed and spent some time there, after that fighting. But not as a group, but they scattered and stayed there as individuals or in small groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D109, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Exhibit 2D03-1189 again, please. Let's turn to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, on page 3, it says that on the occasion of the attack on Prijedor armed groups killed 16 and wounded 16 police and army members. Those were the figures people spoke about in town; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact number, but I remember three persons that I knew who got killed then. But I really cannot be certain about the total number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say that Asim Muhic was in the hamlet of Kadirici and as civilians they mingled with the population in the villages of Asirici [phoen] and Biscani. Then it goes on to say -- to speak about their weapons. Do you -- are you familiar with the events when the army conducted an operation in these villages and found some weapons, and that among the persons taken prisoner then there was some of these persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Zeljaja is? Was he the commander of one of these units?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, then he was commander of the 43rd, or possibly he was in charge of operative affairs. I'm not sure. But he was one of the commanders in the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last page, page 4 of this document. You can see the signature that the criminal report against these persons was filed by Lieutenant-Colonel Milo Zeljaja. It's that person; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I cannot be certain, but I see that that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military court in Banja Luka tried some of these persons for armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I know that there was a military court in Banja Luka, but I'm not familiar with their specific activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, today you were answering the Prosecutor's questions about the -- that event, the killing of those prisoners at Keraterm in the summer of 1992. Do you remember: When you came there, was the road leading to Keraterm blocked by the police, or were you able to reach the entrance freely?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: On the day when we got there, we -- there were no obstacles from the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you arrive at your usual time in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the usual time, at 7.00 or 8.00. I'm not sure. We arrived at the place without hindrance. And after an hour, hour and a half, we left unhindered. But I don't know what happened afterward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There was no police roadblock on the road leading to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: No, there was no roadblock, apart from the guards who were at the entrance, at the gate. There were guards there, but that was the regular state of affairs. I cannot be sure whether they may -- there may have been more of them, but certainly not significantly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see members of the intervention platoon while you were travelling down that road?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: While we were travelling on that road, there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And vehicles were not being stopped; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain whether it was possible to pass freely. We didn't pay attention to these details. I don't know. I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, the Prosecutor asked you about the release of certain persons from Keraterm and what the procedure was. I'm about to show you a document. You said that this was done elsewhere and that you're not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness Exhibit 1D167. That's tab 5 in Mr. Stanisic's Defence binder. Let's wait for the English translation to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, this is a decision of the Crisis Staff dated 2 June - the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality - about the release of imprisoned persons. And let me start this way: It was explained to you that the persons who had been brought to Keraterm were persons suspected of having taken part in combat activities or aided and abetted or took part in some way or other?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I was told that these were persons who are in some way related to combat activities, the arming, or the organisation, or such, that's what we understood them to be, these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here they are called prisoners.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says "prisoners" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at Article 4. All persons over 60 years of age for whom an investigation has confirmed that they did not commit an offence are released. This is basically what you were speaking about when you would find out that somebody was 60. There was nothing left for you to do. It was up to other people to decide about their fate. There was one period when they were being released flat, and later there were problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, that there were some older persons and minors. And in the early stage, there was -- we interviewed them. And once we learned what their age was, they were simply released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there's Article 5. It says: "Other prisoners who may be found not guilty in legal proceedings conducted by competent bodies shall be released ..."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: After this screening by age, we would interview the remaining persons. And if it was our assessment - because we didn't really know - that they took part in anything, they were released because there were no grounds for us to keep them in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here, basically, is the Crisis Staff that defines the criteria for release. They are the ones who decide about that; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know this document. Only later did I learn that there was something. And during the proofing, I believe that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But, basically, you weren't the ones who decided whether a person would be released or kept, and what they would be -- how they would be treated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: We would only forward the information that we had about their activities. In a word, what we knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then the Prosecutor asked you about your knowledge of the conditions at Keraterm. But outside the small area in which you moved from the entrance to your office, you didn't go to the places where the prisoners were kept; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't go there ever. When I said that the conditions were the way they were, I said that that was the information I got from them and -- and what I concluded from the general condition and aspect. They were in a hygienically neglected state, they had beards, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, the Official Notes that you drafted did not include this kind of information, and this was not your job, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: We simply focussed on what I told you I -- we had been doing, and we thought that somebody else was in charge of that, whoever had established the camp and whoever was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you drafted those Official Notes, you and members of your team did not use coercion or force?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: No coercive measures were used. This was just an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Answering the Prosecutor's questions about the arrival, you mentioned that Mr. Bera visited Keraterm on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P601.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, please look at this document carefully. It's a decision by centre chief Stojan Zupljanin to establish a commission to visit the municipalities of Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Sanski Most. And here we have the members of the commission. And Mr. Bera is the commission chairman. You can see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the commission that was set up to investigate the conditions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the drafting of this decision and a little while later, I was not aware of it, and I didn't know about it. And later on I heard that there was a commission that made a report. And I think that in the course of an interview I was shown this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here you mentioned some persons who are in the commission, and now I want to ask you: Do you know Vaso Skondric?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew Vaso but more or less by sight. And later on we did not keep in touch in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ranko Mihic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I knew Ranko Mihic because he worked in the public security station before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Prijedor Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Prijedor Public Security Station. And I think that Mr. Skondric worked somewhere in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Jugoslav Rodic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Jugoslav Rodic was a colleague from the State or National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he worked in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Prijedor detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rodic, you can see here that the task of the commission is to establish whether, in those municipalities, including Prijedor, there were any prisoner of war centres, investigation centres, reception centres, or any other forms in which persons, citizens, are brought in and accommodated; the reason why they were set up; the number of persons brought in, processed, and released; and the ethnic gender and age breakdown of the persons; and the conditions in which they live. Mr. Rodic, did anyone ask you any questions in this part, and do you know that these people actually came there at the time when you were ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Let me see what's written here. I really cannot recall whether they came. But Vojin Bera did come. Now whether, during those visits of his, there were any talks about that, I really can't remember. But maybe he didn't speak about that with me. I simply cannot ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then further down it says that it is necessary to establish whether any citizens moved out from those municipalities, their ethnic background and number, and whether they moved out voluntarily or were forced to move out. Do you remember that there were some activities pertaining to this issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, if you mean the activities of the commission members, I really cannot recall. What I can recall I've already told you, and I don't know anything else, given the place where I was and what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, can we -- can we see - because we don't see it here on the English version - who signed this decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous document, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to P601. I would like the witness to look at the original so that he can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at the last paragraph here. And then, below, it says chief of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the stamp of the centre and the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to go back to P602.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, this is a report on the situation found and issues pertaining to the prisoners or collection centres, the resettlement, and the role of the SJB in relation to these activities. I think that the Prosecutor showed you this document in the course of your interview.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: That was the first time that I saw this document. I think it was in 2003, when I was interviewed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it says here, Pursuant to a decision of the decision of the chief of the Security Services Centre, number 11-141/2, and so on.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- it's -- it is -- it follows up on the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at the last page of this document. That's page 16 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that this document is signed by the commission members, Mr. Vojin Bera.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recognise any of the signatures of the colleagues that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, I might be able to actually recognise Jugoslav Rodic's signature; and perhaps, to an extent, Vojin Bera's. The other two, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to go back to page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, here it says, in the preamble - I will now go through the part that's relevant for the Prijedor municipality - it says here that the armed conflicts in the Prijedor municipality started on the 24th in the Kozarac area and then spread to other areas. So this corresponds to what you knew of the events?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, I've told you -- well, I've told you that this is where -- when the action started and that the reception investigative centres of various shapes and forms were established then, a day or two after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2, it says that in the course of the clashes the Army of the Serbian Republic captured a large number of the members of hostile formations and other persons who were found to be in the areas where armed conflicts went on, and a number of citizens leaving homes and flats sought help and protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move on to the next page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where it says that the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality decided to organise reception and accommodation in the settlement of Trnopolje for persons seeking protection and that prisoners of war should be held for processing in the building of the Keraterm company in Prijedor or in the administrative building and work-shop of the RZR in Omarska. I think it's the mine. It's the iron-ore mine. That's what the acronym stands for. Mr. Rodic, this is more or less what you knew at the time, if you know, from this document, it turns out that the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality set up those centres, Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje alike. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this, the picture is a bit fuller. But I did not know that at the time when all of this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to read out a part of this document that pertains to the situation in Keraterm, the way they describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 3 of this document. And in the English version, that would be page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here we have a description of the facility: The facility of the Keraterm lies along the main Prijedor-Banja Luka road. The facility consists of the rooms of the administration building, offices, halls, restaurants, toilets, and washrooms, and facilities meant for the storage of finished products. The courtyard area is fenced in the way, usual, for work organisations. The entrance is at the main gate on the east side. And on the western side of the facility are auxiliary work premises that have been used since the beginning of the armed conflicts for the accommodation of the Prijedor military police companies -- company. Mr. Rodic, do you know that in Keraterm itself, in the fenced-in area, there was a military police company which also participated in securing the facility?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I know that. I know that there were military police there. I don't know what formation. And I don't know to what extent they participated in securing the facility, if they did at all, but it is a fact that a military police unit was stationed there. I don't know what the composition was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it says here: "Pursuant to a decision of the Prijedor municipality Crisis Staff, the army brought prisoners of war to this facility and the public security station was given the task of securing the facility with employees of the police?" Mr. Rodic, do you know that the police -- or, rather, that pursuant to a decision of the Crisis Staff, the army brought prisoners of war into this part and that the Crisis Staff ordered the police to take part in securing the detention or collection centres, whatever you want to call them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what the basis was for what they did. But based on what I saw there, that the police were mostly stationed around the facility, I did see that, and I think that I saw on some occasions that the military brought in a certain number of persons from the crisis areas by bus, the hot-spots or -- of the activities that they were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then, further down, it says that the conflicts escalated. And I quote: "At the same time, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality assessed that it would be advisable for security reasons to transfer the prisoners to another place and decided on the facilities of the administrative building and work-shops of the Omarska RZR." The same decision, the decision of the Crisis Staff, determined that the Keraterm facility in Prijedor should be used exclusively for transit, that people who had been brought in should be received there solely for the purpose of their transportation to the facilities in Omarska. And then it reads that, on the 27th of May, pursuant to a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality, all the prisoners from the Keraterm facility in Prijedor were transferred to the facility in Omarska. And now there are some things here that are not logical, so please help us out. Did the things that are described in this document really come to pass? Or, in other words, were the prisoners transferred the way it is described in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: What I do know is that after a few days, when we were in Keraterm, there was a transfer to the Omarska area, and I think that I said in the investigative proceedings that I was in the Omarska area for a day or two. But then an order -- or, rather, I can't call it an order, it was a notice for us that the three teams should return to the Keraterm area, where we would engage in investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it says here that - well, it's in the second paragraph; let us go back - that combined investigative teams were set up from the members of national, public, and military security services to operatively process all the prisoners and to determine the degree of their personal responsibility in the fighting. Does that more or less correspond to what you told us about how the combined teams were set up, the joint teams that worked on gathering information about all this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, in the course of this interview and the proofing procedure, I mentioned a couple of times that there were - I'm now talking about Keraterm - the three teams that consisted of the people that they consisted of, the public and national security services, and that, at the beginning, the member -- the representative of the military security was also there, at first a bit more often and later on more seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the task, as indicated here, was to determine the operative processing of all the prisoners and to determine the degree of their personal responsibility in armed combat?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RODIC
utterances.text: Well, what we were doing was we are gathering information about their involvement. That's what we were doing, and that's what I've repeated several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is the right time for our break because I'm about to embark on a new line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I do apologise, Your Honour, just less than one minute, I have to put on the record: We were informed by our learned friend Ms. Paula Lynch that -- and I will quote what he wrote to us: As today's 365th day of our trial, drinks are required, whether they will be in the name of celebration or drowning of sorrows, take your pick. And I wish, also, to express my gratitude to all of our friends from the Interpretation Unit, Technical Unit, as well as the security officers for the last one year of work in this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. And you speak for all of us. We take the adjournment to tomorrow. I believe we're back in this courtroom at 2.15. Mr. Rodic, having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side. And in such meetings and conversations that you have with persons outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we resume tomorrow morning at -- tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of September, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
